title: Croot's proof of Erdős–Graham (unit fractions with denominators in one colour class): the 'smooth numbers + exponential sums' method
connection: Croot (Annals 2003) shows any finite colouring of integers has a monochromatic set with Σ 1/n = 1; the proof uses smooth numbers in an interval and a Fourier/exponential-sum count of subset sums. ES is a 3-term, fixed-numerator version with no colouring freedom.
why: Croot's technology is the most powerful known for 'exact unit-fraction sum' problems; understanding exactly which freedom it needs (many terms, smooth denominators) sharpens what 3-term ES lacks — and whether a 'many-term then merge' route exists (merge identities 1/a + 1/b = 1/c when a+b | ab).
first_step: Read Croot 2003 §2; list the three places where the number of terms is used; check whether any merge lemma (k terms → 3 terms when denominators share structure) can be bolted on; search 'merging unit fractions into three'.
refs: Croot, 'On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions', Ann. Math. 157 (2003)

title: Bloom's density proof of Erdős–Graham (2021) and its Lean formalisation: Fourier-analytic unit fraction counting
connection: Bloom proves every set of positive upper density contains a finite subset with Σ 1/n = 1; formalised in Lean (Bloom–Mehta). The Fourier method counts solutions of Σ 1/n_i = 1 among many candidates.
why: The formalised infrastructure (unit-fraction sums, Fourier counting) is reusable; and Bloom's 'local' lemma (sum = 1 using denominators in a short interval of smooth numbers) may give 'ES over short intervals' statements (e.g. every x ∈ [N, 2N] has 4/x as a sum of ≤ k unit fractions from a prescribed set).
first_step: Read Bloom 2021 Thm 3 and the Lean repository 'unit-fractions'; identify what the key counting proposition gives for *fixed* numerator 4 and 3 terms (probably nothing: it needs many terms); record exactly why.
refs: Bloom, 'On a density conjecture about unit fractions', arXiv:2112.03726

title: Sylvester's 1880 sequence and Egyptian fraction 'denominator growth': why 3-term is the hard case
connection: Sylvester's greedy gives 4/n in ≤ 4 terms always; the gap between 4 (easy, greedy) and 3 (open) is the whole conjecture. Historically, similar 'one fewer term' gaps were closed by divisor-structure lemmas (e.g. Nagell's results on 2/n, 3/n).
why: Revisit how the k = 2 and numerator 2, 3 cases were resolved (they are theorems); the proof pattern for 3/n (always ≤ 2 terms? no: 3/n = 2 terms iff n has a divisor ≡ 2 mod 3; else 3 terms) suggests that ES is the first case where the 'iff' divisor criterion is not local — which is exactly Mordell–Schinzel. Document the exact historical sequence of results.
first_step: Search and read: Nagell 1922/23 on a/n = 1/x + 1/y; Mordell's chapter 30; list which cases (numerator a, k terms) are theorems and by what method.

title: Rhind papyrus 2/n table: did the Egyptian scribes' decomposition rules form a covering system?
connection: The 2/n table decomposes 2/n (odd n ≤ 101) into 2–4 unit fractions by patterns depending on n's factors; scholars (Gillings, Abdulaziz) reconstructed the rules. The structure is a historical 'covering by identities' for numerator 2.
why: Recreational/historical lens; the scribes' choice of 'nice' decompositions (small, even denominators) foreshadows the modern preference for Type I/II; cheap read.
first_step: Read Abdulaziz 'On the Egyptian method of decomposing 2/n into unit fractions' (Historia Math 2008) and note whether any rule there generalises to 4/n with 3 terms.

title: Erdős's own heuristic for ES in 'Some unconventional problems in number theory' and his 'Sierpiński 5/n' remark
connection: Erdős (and Sierpiński for 5/n, Schinzel for a/n with n ≥ n₀(a)) framed the conjecture; Schinzel's generalisation 'a/n in 3 unit fractions for n ≥ n₀(a)' is the natural family. Tools that handle ALL a simultaneously may be forced to use structure invisible for a = 4.
why: The a-family (a/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n ≥ n₀(a)) is a 2-parameter problem; results for specific a (Sierpiński 5/n verified far; Palamà, Yamamoto for a ≤ 36?) and their methods are a direct lead library.
first_step: Search 'Schinzel conjecture a/n three unit fractions n_0(a)' and compile the status table for a ≤ 40 (who proved what, by which identities); check whether any a-value was handled by a non-covering argument.

title: Yamamoto's 1965 proof that odd squares have no Type I/II solutions — read the original for *spare* structure
connection: Yamamoto's argument (reciprocity) is T1. Original papers often contain more than the cited theorem (e.g. a characterisation of which n have f_I = 0).
why: If Yamamoto characterised all n with f_I(n) = 0 (not just squares) the campaign's U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, …} might be explained; also his method's 'failure at squares' may be invertible into a 'success at non-squares' condition.
first_step: Obtain Yamamoto, 'On the Diophantine equation 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z', Mem. Fac. Sci. Kyushu Univ. 19 (1965); read all lemmas; compare with the U(n) sporadic list.

title: Rosati 1954 / Bernstein 1962 / Webb 1970 / Vaughan 1970: trace the lineage of exceptional-set bounds for the 'thin' idea that was dropped
connection: The exceptional-set line (Webb, Vaughan, Elsholtz–Tao, Elsholtz–Planitzer) improved E(N) by better sieving; each paper's 'what we could not do' section records the pointwise obstruction in the author's words.
why: Someone in 1970 may have had an idea for pointwise bounds that was abandoned for being 'too hard', not wrong.
first_step: Read Vaughan 1970 Mathematika §4 (final remarks) and Webb 1970 Proc. AMS; note any conditional or partial pointwise statement.
refs: Vaughan, 'On a problem of Erdős, Straus and Schinzel', Mathematika 17 (1970)

title: Elsholtz–Tao §'open questions' list — re-audit which are now answered and which lead to ES
connection: ET 2013 list several open problems (lower bounds on f(n) for all n? distribution of Type I vs II; polynomial identities). A decade later, some may be resolved in papers not yet in the repo.
why: Cheap literature update with precise targets.
first_step: Re-read ET §1.3–1.4 'open problems'; for each, search arXiv 2013–2026 (citations of ET via Semantic Scholar) and note status.

title: Ask Christian Elsholtz / Stefan Planitzer directly what they consider the current frontier
connection: People item: the authors of the almost-all lower bound f(n) ≥ (log n)^{log 6 + o(1)} are the closest active experts; a short email with the campaign's barrier map attached could elicit either a known dead-end or a tip.
why: Human expert input is cheap relative to the search cost; the campaign's FRONTIER.md is a ready-made attachment.
first_step: Draft a 10-line email summarising the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) and asking (i) is this reduction known, (ii) any route they abandoned; send.
refs: Elsholtz–Planitzer, 'Egyptian fractions and the Erdős–Straus conjecture' (Monatsh. Math 2020?)

title: Post the single-integer lower tail as a MathOverflow question
connection: FRONTIER §2's reduction ('a specific integer tied to p must have a divisor in a class with modulus part of the solution') is a clean, citable question for MO: 'Is there any known theorem giving ≥1 divisor in a tied residue class for every n?'
why: MO has answered 'is there any theorem of shape X' questions well (experts recall obscure results); low cost.
first_step: Write the MO question with the precise statement (4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C for some C), the heuristic count log²p, and the known results (Lenstra upper bound, almost-all results); post under number-theory tag.

title: Pólya–Vinogradov-era people: ask Igor Shparlinski about divisor-restricted modular hyperbola points
connection: Shparlinski has many papers on modular hyperbolas and on divisors in residue classes; the exact ES-shaped question (points on xy ≡ −1 mod e with x,y | N) is in his wheelhouse.
why: People item; cheap; he may know a relevant character-sum bound or a reason it's hopeless.
first_step: Email with the e-slice formulation; ask whether 'hyperbola points with both coordinates dividing a given N' has been studied.

title: Contact Bright and Loughran about an integral-Brauer–Manin *refinement* at the ES fibre
connection: BL showed no BM obstruction; the campaign found the Brauer class dies at the ES fibre k = 0. Ask them whether any finer invariant (descent obstruction, étale-Brauer, or 'integral points on log K3 / cubic surfaces with 3 A₁ singularities') applies to U_n.
why: The surface people know what finer obstructions exist; cheap to ask.
first_step: Email summarising Z52_BANKED 'why the obvious Brauer class dies at k = 0'; ask about étale-Brauer and about Harpaz–Wittenberg fibration method for integral points.

title: Thomas Bloom's unit-fractions Lean library as a base for an 'ES data' formal verification
connection: The Bloom–Mehta Lean project has definitions for unit fraction sums; a formally verified 'ES holds for all n ≤ 10⁶ via these certificates' would be a small but citable deliverable and a test of mathlib infrastructure.
why: Formal verification of computations is now routine; cheap.
first_step: Clone the unit-fractions repo; write a `decide`/`native_decide` based checker for 4/n certificates for n ≤ 10⁴ first.

title: Conference lens: which 2026–27 meetings have unit fractions / Egyptian fractions sessions (Integers, CANT, ELAZ)?
connection: CANT (Combinatorial and Additive Number Theory, NYC), the INTEGERS conference, and ELAZ host unit-fraction talks regularly; abstracts there may contain unpublished partial results.
why: Cheap scan.
first_step: Fetch the abstracts of CANT 2024–2026 and INTEGERS 2025; grep for 'unit fraction', 'Egyptian', 'Straus'.

title: Mordell's chapter 30 'the equation 4/n' — the discarded alternative parametrisations
connection: Mordell lists several families beyond the mod-840 ones and remarks on their limitations; the discarded families may be non-polynomial in disguise.
why: Primary-source check; the campaign cites Mordell via secondary literature.
first_step: Read Mordell ch. 30 fully; transcribe every identity and its residue class; compare with the repo's identity census (git grep -il 'identit' -- 'DISCOVERIES.md').

title: Stewart–Tijdeman / Bleicher: 'Egyptian fractions with denominators in a bounded set of prime factors' (S-unit viewpoint)
connection: Restrict x,y,z to S-units (or to numbers with prime factors from a set S); 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z becomes an S-unit equation xy + yz + zx = (4/n)xyz with finitely many solutions (Evertse). For varying n, the count is tied to S.
why: S-unit theory gives finiteness + effective bounds (Baker); ES wants infinitude across n, but the S-unit lens might explain the preferred shapes of solutions (denominators smooth relative to p).
first_step: Compute the smoothness of (x,y,z)/p-part for the first solution of each p ≤ 10⁶; are the non-p parts typically (log p)-smooth? If so, the S-unit equation over a fixed S ∪ {p} is the right finite problem per p.

title: Geometry of numbers: Minkowski's theorem on the 'Type II' lattice to force a divisor pair
connection: Type II: ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd. For fixed (c,d), the set {(f, f′)} is a congruence sublattice; Minkowski's theorem guarantees a nonzero lattice point in any convex body of volume 2^k det Λ; the hyperbola ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 is not convex, but regions between hyperbolas are.
why: Pigeonhole/Minkowski is the classic 'existence for every n' tool (two-squares theorem); it fails here because the target is a single hyperbola, but a 'union over (c,d)' body might have enough volume. Quantify.
first_step: For fixed p, compute the total 'volume' Σ_{(c,d) ≤ X} (area of the region 4c²dp < ff′ < 4c²dp + 2 inside the congruence conditions) vs the lattice determinant; see at which X Minkowski-type volume exceeds the threshold (expect: never by a polylog factor — document the gap).

title: Thue's lemma / Brillhart-style two-squares proof pattern applied to p² + 4c²d
connection: The two-squares theorem's elementary proofs (Thue's lemma: for a² ≡ −1 mod p find small x,y with x ≡ ay mod p) produce a divisor from a square root. Type I needs f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd; i.e. a 'square root of −4c²d' structure.
why: Thue's lemma is the canonical rigidity mechanism (R) that produces a pointwise divisor; the question is whether the congruence f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) can be built into the lattice.
first_step: Fix c,d; the condition is f | p² + 4c²d ⟺ p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f); if −4c²d is a QR mod f, Thue gives a representation f·k = u² + 4c²d v² with small u,v; check whether choosing f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) is compatible with the Thue box.

title: Binary quadratic forms: Type I as representation of p² by a form of discriminant −16c²d
connection: f | p² + 4c²d means p² + 4c²d = f·g; representation theory of binary quadratic forms (Gauss composition) describes which f occur as 'first coefficients' of forms representing p² + 4c²d... Equivalently, (p, c·2√(−d)) is a vector in an imaginary quadratic order; the norm factorisation is governed by the class group of ℚ(√−d).
why: Class-group structure of ℤ[√−d] is *rigid* and the 'divisor in a residue class' condition on f may translate into a *genus* condition (which is a character condition, computable), leaving the class-group part.
first_step: Write the Type I condition in the order O_d = ℤ[2c√−d]: f is the norm of an ideal dividing (p + 2c√−d)? Check: N(p + 2c√−d) = p² + 4c²d. So f | N(α) for α = p + 2c√−d; ideal divisors of (α) have norms f; the residue condition f ≡ −p mod 4cd is a condition on the ideal class modulo 4cd (ray class group). Verify this translation numerically.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Gauss composition / Bhargava cubes for the Type II identity ff′ − 4c²dp = 1
connection: ff′ − (2c)²dp = 1 is a 'norm form equals 1' type equation: ff′ − D·1 = 1 with D = 4c²dp; i.e. the matrix [[f, 2c√d],[2c√d·p... ]] — more precisely it says f·f′ ≡ 1 mod 4c²dp. Bhargava's parametrisation of ideal classes by 2×2×2 cubes might organise the triples (f, f′, 4c²d) with product structure.
why: Composition laws give group structure on solution sets of quadratic-type equations; a group structure on ES certificates for fixed p would be a huge structural input (cf. Markoff).
first_step: Check whether the set of Type II certificates for fixed p carries a natural binary operation (e.g. via the ideal (f, p + 2c√−d) composition); test on p = 1009: list certificates and look for closure.

title: Ray class fields and the splitting of p in ℚ(√−d, ζ_{4cd}): ES certificates as Frobenius conditions
connection: The condition 'an ideal of norm f dividing (p + 2c√−d) has f ≡ −p (mod 4cd)' is a condition on Frobenius of f in a ray class field mod 4cd of ℚ(√−d). Chebotarev gives density; ES needs existence for one (c,d) at each p.
why: Chebotarev-type existence for one prime p (not density) is where effective Chebotarev + GRH gives 'a prime of norm ≤ (log disc)²' — Lagarias–Odlyzko. But here f is not required prime, and the field depends on (c,d), so a *family* of ray class fields indexed by (c,d) is probed at the single prime p. Family versions of Chebotarev (e.g. Kowalski's large sieve for Frobenius) give almost-all; pointwise is the open shape.
first_step: Write the exact Frobenius statement for the Type I condition; check in Sage for p = 1009 and small (c,d) that the ray class description matches the divisor form; then search 'Chebotarev for a fixed prime over a family of fields'.
refs: Kowalski, The large sieve and its applications

title: Hilbert's irreducibility / thin sets: the set of p for which a fixed (c,d) fails is 'thin' in what sense?
connection: For each (c,d), the set of p with no divisor f of p² + 4c²d in class −p mod 4cd is a set defined by factorisation conditions on a quadratic polynomial in p; the intersection over all (c,d) is the counterexample set. Thin-set theory (Serre) describes such sets as images of covers.
why: Hilbert irreducibility gives 'most p are not in the thin set'; the exact intersection structure over infinitely many (c,d) is a 'infinite intersection of thin sets is empty' question — a shape with some precedent (e.g. in Zaremba's structure).
first_step: Formulate 'fail(c,d)' as a condition on the factorisation of the quadratic polynomial P_{c,d}(p) = p² + 4c²d; check whether fail(c,d) is contained in a thin set in Serre's sense (likely not, it's a factorisation condition not a cover condition); record.
refs: Serre, Topics in Galois Theory ch. 3

title: Probabilistic method with alterations on the (c,d) grid: a second-moment bound for the tied-modulus count for an *explicit* subfamily of p
connection: Second-moment (Chebyshev) + alterations proves existence for almost all p; the question is whether for *structured* p (e.g. p = 1 + 24m with m having all small primes as factors) the variance is small enough to prove f(p) ≥ 1 unconditionally.
why: 'Almost all' results can sometimes be upgraded to 'all p in an explicit sparse set', which would be a new infinite case of ES (the campaign says no infinite case is proved! Though Mordell identities cover residue classes… those are infinite sets of n but not of primes? Mordell's identities DO cover infinitely many primes; what is open is only square classes). So the target: an explicit infinite set of primes inside the square classes mod 840.
first_step: Check FRONTIER §5 for what is known about explicit infinite subsets of hard primes; then try: primes p with p ≡ 1 mod 840 and 4p+1 ≡ 0 mod 5 … construct a sub-family where a fixed C wins by a *non-polynomial* reason (e.g. p such that 4p + 1 is 5 × a prime ≡ −1 mod 4? that's a prime-value condition, not a residue class — and indeed gives infinitely many p conditionally on Dickson).

title: Explicit infinite family inside the square classes via Bateman–Horn-free arguments: p with 4p+1 having a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4
connection: 4p + 1 (C = 1) has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4 iff 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 (since 4p+1 ≡ 1 mod 4, it has an even number of such factors, so ≥ 2 if any; any prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 is itself a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4). So C = 1 wins iff 4p + 1 is not a product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 — i.e. iff 4p+1 is not a sum of two squares in the 'all factors 1 mod 4' sense.
why: This is a clean, non-polynomial criterion: ES(p) holds whenever 4p+1 is not entirely composed of primes ≡ 1 mod 4. The complementary set (4p+1 all of whose prime factors are ≡ 1 mod 4) has density → 0 (Landau–Ramanujan-type, ~ 1/√log p). Likewise C = 2: 8p+1 not all factors ≡ 1 mod 8 ... each C removes a 1/√log-density set; the intersection is the real target. Document this chain explicitly as the cleanest statement of 'why the heuristic count is log²p but no proof'.
first_step: Verify the claim (C = 1 Type II wins iff 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4) against the repo's divisor form; compute the density of primes p ≤ 10⁷ with 4p+1 having only factors ≡ 1 mod 4; then for C=1..K the joint density.

title: Primes p for which 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1, … are all 'sums of two squares type': structure of the joint exceptional set
connection: Following the C=1 criterion: the failure set for C ≤ K is {p : for every C ≤ K, 4Cp + 1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C}. For C with 4C having few residue classes ≡ −1 the condition is 'all prime factors in a subgroup' — a multiplicative-structure condition (like 'n is a norm from ℚ(i)').
why: Norm-type sets have Dirichlet-series descriptions (Landau), so the joint failure set for C ≤ K has a computable density ~ Π_C (1 − something)^(…) and a *structure* (a norm from a compositum?). If the joint failure set for all C were provably empty by a norm argument… that's ES. But at least the per-C structure is exact.
first_step: For C = 1,2,3: characterise 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' exactly in terms of prime factorisation (subgroup H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× not containing −1 and all factors in H_C? Not quite — subset products must avoid −1, which for a subgroup H ∌ −1 means all factors in H; else more complex). Tabulate for C ≤ 10.

title: Is 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' equivalent to 'all prime factors lie in a −1-free subgroup' when the subset-product set is a subgroup? (structure lemma)
connection: Subset products of the prime factors of N generate a submonoid of (ℤ/4C)^×; since the group is finite, the submonoid is a subgroup H; −1 ∉ H iff N's factors generate a −1-free subgroup. So 'C fails for p' ⟺ the prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup of (ℤ/4C)^× not containing −1 — IF the subset-product set (with multiplicities) equals the generated subgroup, which needs enough multiplicity. With multiplicity-1 factors it's only the 'subset products', a subset of H.
why: Clarifying exactly when 'generated subgroup' = 'subset product set' (gate G4 in the repo) matters: if the gap is empirically negligible, the failure condition is a clean Galois condition (all factors split in a certain abelian extension), i.e. ES ⟺ 'for some C, 4Cp+1 has a prime factor inert in a subfield' — a Chebotarev-at-a-point shape.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 50: compute both (subgroup generated contains −1) and (subset product set contains −1); count disagreements.

title: Kummer/Galois reformulation: ES ⟸ ∃C: some prime factor q of 4Cp+1 has Frobenius outside a fixed subgroup of Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ)
connection: If the subgroup criterion holds, then C wins whenever some prime q | 4Cp+1 has q mod 4C ∉ H for every −1-free subgroup H... Simplest: q ≡ −1 mod 4C directly (then q itself is the divisor). So a sufficient condition: 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C. Over C, this is 'the polynomial values 4Cp+1 (C varying, p fixed) have a prime factor in the class −1' — a statement about prime divisors of a linear polynomial in C at a fixed 'twist' p.
why: Prime divisors of values of linear forms in residue classes is a well-studied topic (e.g. Bang–Zsigmondy for a^n − 1, and 'prime factors of n! ± 1' type results); the fixed-p twist is unusual but concrete.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest C such that 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C (the 'prime-divisor' certificate); compare to C_min; search 'prime divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C'.

title: Erdős–Kac for the number of prime factors of 4Cp+1 across C at fixed p: 'enough factors' heuristics
connection: The subset-product set is large when ω(4Cp+1) is large; the distribution of ω over C ≤ X at fixed p is Erdős–Kac-like (normal with mean log log). Some C have ω ≥ 2 log log; for those the subset-product set likely covers (ℤ/4C)^×... except a subgroup obstruction.
why: Separates 'few factors' (bad luck) from 'wrong subgroup' (structural) failure types; the structural type is the one a proof must address.
first_step: Classify failures of (p, C) for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 100 into: ω ≤ 1; subgroup generated by factors misses −1; subgroup contains −1 but subset-products miss. Tabulate.

title: Analogy with the 'least prime quadratic non-residue' problem: existence of ONE prime with a prescribed Legendre symbol
connection: Vinogradov's least-QNR problem asks for a prime q ≤ p^ε with (q/p) = −1 — a pointwise statement about one prime, proved via Burgess bounds (unconditionally q ≪ p^{1/(4√e)+ε}). ES needs one prime factor of some 4Cp+1 with a prescribed residue mod 4C — same flavour: 'one object with a prescribed character value'.
why: Burgess's method is a genuine pointwise technique for character values; the campaign's barrier notes say gate G4 'needs Vinogradov's conjecture' — but perhaps a Burgess-strength version suffices for a *weaker* ES-adjacent statement (e.g. ES for p with an extra parameter).
first_step: Formulate: is there a C ≤ p^θ such that 4Cp+1 has a prime factor q ≡ −1 mod 4C? Heuristically trivial for large θ (many C), but a Burgess-type proof would need to control characters mod 4C over C — the modulus varies with C. Check whether a 'variable modulus Burgess' (e.g. Heath-Brown's large sieve for real characters) gives it.
refs: Heath-Brown, 'A mean value estimate for real character sums' (1995)

title: Heath-Brown's large sieve for real characters applied to the family {χ_{4C}} at the fixed point p
connection: Heath-Brown's quadratic large sieve bounds Σ_C |Σ_n a_n (n/4C)|² over square-free C; with a_n supported on n = 4Cp+1... hmm the inner sum depends on C. Alternative: fix p, sum over C of the character sum Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ(d) for χ mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1 — the M_BM main term.
why: The campaign's M_BM is a sum over C of twisted divisor sums; a large-sieve input over C would control the *error* in the mean value, i.e. R(p) ≈ M_BM(p) — exactly the needed lower tail but only on average over p. Document the exact loss.
first_step: Read FRONTIER §2's M_BM derivation; identify the error term; check whether Heath-Brown's bound applies with the roles of modulus and argument as they are.

title: Linnik's theorem and its 'one prime in an AP' nature as the template for 'one divisor in a class'
connection: Linnik: the least prime in an AP mod q is ≤ q^L. It's a pointwise (for every q) statement with polylog... no, with a *power* of q reservoir. ES's reservoir is the divisors of ONE number — but over C there are infinitely many numbers 4Cp+1. Reframe: is there a 'Linnik for shifted multiples': for every p, some C ≤ p^A has 4Cp+1 with a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C?
why: With C up to p^A the reservoir IS power-sized, so Linnik-type methods (zero-density, log-free) might apply — this is a *different* (weaker-looking but still ES-implying) target the repo's B3 critique may not cover, since the certificate count over C ≤ p^A is ≫ p^{A−o(1)}... wait, does C ≤ p^A keep the count polylog? The expected number of winning C ≤ X is ≈ Σ_{C≤X} 1/φ(4C)·(something) ≈ log X·const — still only log. Hmm: that's the campaign's point (B3). But Linnik's problem ALSO has only ~q^L/φ(q)·(1/log) expected primes... no, it has many. Record the count honestly and still try: the *prime-divisor* certificate count over C ≤ p^A.
first_step: Compute E[#{C ≤ X: 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C}] empirically for p ≈ 10⁶ and X up to 10⁶; fit log X vs power growth.

title: Erdős's 'covering congruences' letters and the Erdős–Selfridge sign heuristics as hints for which modulus families to try
connection: Erdős proposed many covering-type conjectures; his letters to Selfridge (published partially) contain rules of thumb for when covering fails; a historian's reading may give the exact reason Erdős believed ES was 'not provable by congruences alone'.
why: History-of-ideas item; cheap.
first_step: Search 'Erdős Straus conjecture congruences cannot suffice Erdős remark' and read Erdős–Graham 'Old and new problems' §on unit fractions for Erdős's own assessment.
refs: Erdős–Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980)

title: Monks–Moore style 'hypergraph' of Egyptian-fraction decompositions and Hall's marriage theorem
connection: Hall's theorem gives existence of systems of distinct representatives from counting conditions; for the family of sets S_C = {divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C}, ES needs ONE non-empty set, not an SDR — a much weaker requirement. But Hall-type 'defect' versions (König) give lower bounds on how many sets are non-empty from global counts.
why: Trivial direction: Σ_C |S_C| ≥ 1 ⟹ some S_C ≠ ∅; the campaign's M_BM is exactly the average of Σ_C |S_C| over p. The marriage-theorem lens asks instead for *structural* reasons (a bipartite graph between C's and divisor classes with a perfect matching for all p) — equivalent to a 'universal' witness assignment.
first_step: Note that it reduces to the counting statement; record as a reminder that 'structure beyond counting' is what's needed; cheap to drop.

title: Ramanujan's 'highly composite' intuition: do primes p for which 4Cp+1 is highly composite for some small C always have solutions trivially? (converse direction for hard primes)
connection: Hard primes should be those for which 4Cp+1 has few prime factors for all small C — i.e. p such that 4Cp+1 is prime or nearly prime for C = 1..K. 'Prime-producing' primes p (4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1 all prime) are rare (Hardy–Littlewood) but infinitely many conjecturally; are those the only hard ones?
why: If hardness ⟺ 'all 4Cp+1 are nearly prime' then ES failure needs a 'prime constellation' of unbounded length — impossible by sieve upper bounds! (Any fixed length is fine, but failing at ALL C ≤ K with K → ∞ needs 4Cp+1 ∈ {prime or product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4C...}.) Check whether the 'all nearly prime' heuristic for failure matches data.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁷, correlate C_min(p) with Σ_{C ≤ 10} ω(4Cp+1); check whether large C_min ⟺ small ω's.

title: Upper-bound sieve as a positive tool: 'not all of 4Cp+1 (C ≤ K) can be prime' is provable — can 'not all can avoid class −1 mod 4C' be?
connection: Brun's sieve proves that among 4Cp+1, C ≤ K (K ≈ (log p)^A), not all are prime (indeed at most O(K/log p) are). The ES failure condition per C is weaker than primality (products of primes in a −1-free subgroup), but still a 'sifted' condition; the sieve gives an upper bound on how many C can have 4Cp+1 with ALL prime factors in a given subgroup H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× (a Landau-type sieve, density 1/√log for index-2 H).
why: Upper-bound sieves (unlike lower-bound) are robust and pointwise in p! If the upper bound on #{C ≤ K : all prime factors of 4Cp+1 in H_C} is < K, we get a C that wins — a genuinely pointwise argument. The catch: H_C varies with C and the sieve dimension is ~1/2 per C, giving bound ≈ K/√(log p)... times a constant; if the constant is < 1 we win! Must check: does a Selberg upper-bound sieve over the SHORT interval of C ≤ K with p ≈ huge give K · Π (1 − 1/2q) ≈ K/√log K, not K/√log p — since the sieving primes relevant up to K only. Then the bound is K/√log K < K, trivially fine — but it only bounds those C with no SMALL (≤ K) prime factor outside H; larger prime factors are unsifted. So the argument fails without input on large prime factors. Record precisely.
first_step: Write the sifted set precisely: F_C(p) = 'every prime factor q of 4Cp+1 satisfies q ∈ H_C' where H_C is the subgroup generated... (H_C depends on all factors, circular — fix H_C = a maximal −1-free subgroup instead, which for 4C = 4 is {1 mod 4}). Then bound #{C ≤ K: 4Cp+1 ∈ ℕ_{H}} via Selberg with sieve dimension 1/2 restricted to primes ≤ z; compute the numeric bound for p = 10¹⁸, K = 10⁶, z = 10⁶ and see how far it is from K.

title: Fermat's descent / Vieta jumping on U_n via the 'swap two coordinates' and 'reflect in the third' involutions
connection: U_n: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx). Solving for z: z = nxy/(4xy − n(x+y)); not a quadratic in z, so no Vieta involution in z directly. But in the homogenised cubic surface there may be involutions via lines on the surface (a cubic surface has 27 lines; the lines through a rational point give conic-bundle involutions).
why: Conic-bundle structure on the cubic surface U_n gives a fibration whose fibres are conics; integral points on conics over ℤ are classical (Legendre); a 'descent along conic fibres' is an ES-specific tool not yet tried? (git grep conic).
first_step: Find the 27 lines of the projective closure of U_n (it's singular, so fewer); pick a conic bundle; write the conic over ℚ(t) and the integrality condition; test for p = 1009 whether integer points lie on few conic fibres.

title: Lines on the ES cubic surface: do the lines correspond to the known polynomial identities?
connection: Polynomial identities (Mordell families) are rational curves on U_n parametrised by n; lines on the cubic surface are the simplest rational curves. Conjecture: each degree-1 identity in n is a line, and Mordell–Schinzel's non-existence on square classes is a statement that no line defined over the function field ℚ(n) meets the integral locus there.
why: Translates the 'identities' question into the (finite!) geometry of 27 lines; new identities might be found among non-obvious lines or conics (degree-2 rational curves).
first_step: Compute the lines on 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) over ℚ(n) in Sage/Magma; match with the known identity list.

title: Rational curves of higher degree on U_n/ℚ(n) with floor/sqrt: 'Puiseux identities'
connection: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities (rational curves over ℚ(n)) on square classes. But identities over ℚ(√n) (i.e. n = m² and x,y,z polynomials in m) are allowed and exist (the m² case has solutions from m). The question for primes: identities over ℚ(n^{1/k}) are not applicable since p is not a k-th power — but identities over ℚ(√(n+a)) could apply when n+a is a square. A 'union over a' cover? Each a covers a sparse set (n = m² − a), total density 0 — so no, unless a varies with n. Record and drop? Keep as an item: 'Schinzel's theorem for algebraic-function identities'.
why: Clarifies what algebraic-function identities can and cannot do; Schinzel may have covered it.
first_step: Search 'Schinzel identities Erdős–Straus algebraic function of n'; read Schinzel 2000 'On sums of three unit fractions with polynomial denominators'.

title: Jacobsthal function analogue: longest run of C with 4Cp+1 'bad'
connection: The Jacobsthal function j(m) is the longest gap between integers coprime to m; here, define J(p) = C_min(p) − 1 = the longest initial run of bad C. Jacobsthal-type upper bounds (Iwaniec: j(m) ≪ log²m) are *pointwise*, proved by sieve.
why: If 'bad C' could be modelled as 'C hitting a residue class mod each small prime' (like non-coprimality), Iwaniec's method would bound C_min(p) ≪ log²p pointwise — a proof! The model is wrong (badness is not a congruence condition in C) but the degree of mismatch is the question.
first_step: Test empirically whether badness of C is 'locally determined': for fixed p, is the set of bad C periodic mod small moduli? (Compute correlation of bad(C) with C mod q.)

title: Carmichael's λ and the group structure of (ℤ/4C)^× : choosing C with (ℤ/4C)^× cyclic of small order to make −1 'easy to hit'
connection: For C = 1: (ℤ/4)^× = {±1}; a single factor ≡ 3 mod 4 suffices. For C = p': (ℤ/4p')^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(p'−1). −1 is the unique element of order 2 in the cyclic part… the chance a random subset product hits −1 is ≈ 1/φ(4C) per product, but the number of products is 2^ω. Choosing C with φ(4C) small relative to 2^{ω(4Cp+1)}: C prime-power-ish and 4Cp+1 very composite.
why: Optimising the choice of C-family by group structure is a cheap heuristic refinement; could yield a family of C where the win probability is bounded below (e.g. C with 4C | something).
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, among winning C ≤ 10⁴, histogram φ(4C)/2^{ω(4Cp+1)}.

title: Choose C = (p−1)/4 or C = (p+3)/4 etc.: 'self-referential' C that make 4Cp+1 factor algebraically
connection: If C is a polynomial in p, 4Cp + 1 is a polynomial in p which may factor: e.g. C = p gives 4p² + 1 (irreducible); C = (p² − 1)/4 ... gives p³ − p + 1; C = 2p+1... Algebraic factorisations give guaranteed divisors; the residue condition then is a polynomial congruence — i.e. this IS the polynomial-identity route (B1), but with quadratic/cubic C. Mordell–Schinzel covers all polynomial C? It covers polynomial x,y,z; polynomial C ⟹ polynomial (x,y,z). So yes.
why: Still worth listing: identities with C = polynomial of degree ≥ 3 are not in Mordell's table, and the theorem forbids them only on square classes — maybe they cover *more* of the non-square classes (reducing the residual set to exactly the squares mod a larger modulus?).
first_step: Enumerate C = aP(p) for small polynomials P of degree ≤ 3, factor 4Cp+1 symbolically, check which residue classes mod 840·k get covered.

title: Erdős–Straus for Gaussian integers / over ℤ[i]: does the analogue hold and does its proof (if any) use something ES lacks?
connection: ES over ℤ[i]: 4/α = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with Gaussian integers; the extra units and the splitting of p ≡ 1 mod 4 (p = ππ̄) change the problem: for p ≡ 1 mod 4, 4/p = (4/π)(1/π̄) — the hard primes split! The question 4/π for a Gaussian prime π of norm p.
why: Over ℤ[i] the analogue might be easier (more structure) or provably different; comparing sheds light on what ℤ lacks. Repo may have this (git grep Gaussian).
first_step: git grep -il 'gaussian integer' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute solutions of 4/π = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z over ℤ[i] for norm(π) ≤ 10⁴ with |x|,|y|,|z| ≤ N(π)² and see whether every π has one.
refs: BRAINSTORM/ (Gaussian normalisation noted in z52 synthesis)

title: Function-field ES (F_q[T]) proved variants: extract the exact mechanism and ask what the number-field analogue of that mechanism is
connection: Repo notes ES over F_q[T] has proved variants. The proof mechanism there (likely: polynomial identities suffice because 'squares' are handled by the Frobenius / q-th powers or by abundance of irreducibles in classes) is the thing to translate.
why: If the function-field proof uses *only* covering identities plus a case that is special to char p (e.g. T ↦ T^q), then the number-field obstruction is exactly 'no Frobenius'; if it uses counting with power-size reservoir (Riemann hypothesis for curves), then that's the (T) mechanism.
first_step: git grep -il 'F_q\[T\]\|function field' -- '*.md' to find the repo's statement and the reference; read the proof; write a 1-paragraph 'mechanism extraction'.

title: ES in ℤ/mℤ for all m (local solvability) as a finite-automaton: compute the minimal m where local information already determines 'how many lifts'
connection: Local solvability is trivial (Bright–Loughran), but the *number* of solutions mod m with lifting structure (Hensel) gives a 'local density' σ_m(p); the product over m of σ_m is the singular series. For fixed p, the singular series Π_q σ_q(p) is an explicit function of p's residues; its size vs the actual f(p) is the 'global vs local' gap.
why: Singular-series-to-actual-count ratios are informative; if f(p)/S(p) concentrates, the hard part is the archimedean/size part, not local arithmetic.
first_step: Compute S(p) = Π_{q ≤ 100} σ_q(p) with σ_q = (# solutions mod q)/q² and compare to f(p) for p ≤ 10⁵; regress.

title: Egyptian fraction 'Engel expansion' and 'Pierce expansion' of 4/p: alternative canonical expansions with ≤ 3 terms?
connection: Engel expansion writes x = 1/a₁ + 1/(a₁a₂) + 1/(a₁a₂a₃) + …; Pierce alternates signs. For 4/p, the Engel expansion's length and the possibility of truncation/modification to 3 unit fractions is an unexplored canonical form.
why: Canonical expansions with algebraic structure (Engel: a_{k+1} determined by a_k) might make 'length 3' a tractable condition like ES₅'s CF length.
first_step: Compute Engel expansions of 4/p for p ≤ 10⁴; count lengths; check whether a length-3 Engel expansion exists for all p (unlikely) or whether the Engel denominators relate to Type I/II parameters.

title: Stern–Brocot / Farey neighbours: 4/p's Farey parents and the two-term splitting 4/p = 1/x + (4x−p)/(px)
connection: Farey neighbours a/b, c/d with bc − ad = 1 give 1/(bd) = c/d − a/b; a unit-fraction-friendly structure. Writing 4/p as a sum of unit fractions via Farey-neighbour chains of length 3.
why: The repo has Farey items (bsA_farey_*); the free-lane twist: is there a 'Farey path' interpretation where ES = path of length 3 in the Farey graph from 4/p to 0 with unit-fraction steps? That's close to the CF/ES₅ form; worth making explicit.
first_step: git grep -il farey BRAINSTORM | head; then compute for p ≤ 1000 the Farey-graph distance from 4/p to 0 under 'subtract a unit fraction' moves.

title: Music/tilings: 4/p as a rhythm — Euclidean rhythms and unit-fraction tilings of the circle
connection: Tiling a circle of circumference 4 by three arcs of lengths p/x, p/y, p/z... i.e. 4 = p/x + p/y + p/z — a tiling of [0,4] by rational lengths with a common 'p' numerator. Euclidean rhythms (Toussaint) relate to Bjorklund's algorithm = Euclid's algorithm = continued fractions.
why: Recreational lens that lands on continued fractions again; perhaps a rhythmic 'evenness' measure corresponds to CF length ≤ 3.
first_step: Just note the reformulation; compute whether the Bjorklund rhythm E(4, p) decomposes into 3 'regular' sub-rhythms iff ES solution exists with specific structure — 15 minutes.
refs: Toussaint, 'The Euclidean algorithm generates traditional musical rhythms' (2005)

title: Rep-tiles and squared rectangles: 4/n as a dissection of a rectangle into three rectangles with integer aspect ratios
connection: A rectangle of aspect ratio 4/n cut into three rectangles of aspect ratios 1/x, 1/y, 1/z (stacked); Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte's electrical-network dissection theory (Kirchhoff) turns dissections into resistor networks — connecting to the resistor item.
why: Dissection theory has a determinant (Kirchhoff) formalism that counts dissections exactly; a 3-piece dissection existence theorem might have a direct proof.
first_step: Formalise: stacked rectangles of widths w and heights h_i with w/h_i = x... (does the sum of three unit fractions correspond to a 3-rectangle stack? 4/n = Σ 1/x_i is 'height' addition for unit width: heights 1/x_i, total 4/n — trivially yes); so the geometric content is nil unless we require a *squared* dissection. Drop unless squared-rectangle theory gives something.

title: Games: ES as a two-player game (Adversary picks p, Prover picks C, Adversary reveals factorisation...) and its game value
connection: Formulate the proof search as a game to apply game-theoretic/learning-theoretic bounds: Prover's strategy = a (possibly adaptive) sequence of C's; Adversary = the integers. The minimal 'strategy depth' is C_min's worst case.
why: Meta-reformulation; it frames adaptive strategies (choose next C based on factorisation of 4C₁p+1) which are not covering systems — the adaptive route has been underexplored.
first_step: Design an adaptive strategy: C₁ = 1; if 4p+1 = Π q_i (all ≡ 1 mod 4), set C₂ = q₁ (a prime factor), check 4q₁p+1; etc. Test whether adaptive depth is smaller than C_min for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Adaptive C-choice using the factorisation of the previous failure: C_{k+1} = a prime factor of 4C_k p + 1
connection: If q | 4Cp+1 then 4qp·(something)... consider C′ = Cq: 4Cqp + 1 ≡ 1 − q·(4Cp) ... hmm; since 4Cp ≡ −1 mod q, 4Cq'p+1 for C' = C·k ≡ 1 − k mod q. Choosing k ≡ 1 mod q gives q | 4C'p+1 again with a different cofactor — a way to 'reuse' a prime factor q and search the cofactor's residue. This builds chains of C sharing factors: a tree search with algebraic guidance.
why: Algebraically guided chains may hit −1 mod 4C' faster than blind enumeration; and chain structure might be provable (like Euclid's algorithm steps).
first_step: Implement the chain rule and measure chain length to success vs C_min for p ≤ 10⁶.
